opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it came down to a simple calculation I made pretty early on, even if I couldn't have explained it this clearly at the time.

Everyone around me, teachers, parents, relatives, was saying the same thing: your strong subjects are already good, so the efficient move is to pour your time into the weak ones, because that's where the points are. On paper that makes sense. The exam is a total score, and pulling a weak subject up is usually easier than pushing a strong one higher.

But when I looked at how I actually spent my days, I noticed something. When I worked on the things I was good at and loved, I had energy. I'd lose track of time, go way beyond the syllabus, and come out feeling more like myself. When I forced myself to grind on the weak subjects, I was miserable, and the gains were small. I'd get a few more points and feel like I'd traded away something more valuable.

So I asked myself what I was optimizing for. If it was just the name of the university, then sure, fix the weak spots. But I had a feeling that what would matter later in life wasn't being average-to-good at everything. It was being really, unusually good at a few things. The world doesn't reward you much for having no weaknesses. It rewards you for having a real strength that's sharp enough to matter.

I also didn't want to lose that early instinct, the curiosity that pulls you toward certain things. I think a lot of people have it as kids, and the system slowly trains it out of them by telling them to fix their "deficiencies" over and over. Once you lose it, it's very hard to get back.

Was it a risk? Definitely. I probably gave up some options, and there were moments I wondered whether I was just being stubborn. But looking back, I'd make the same choice. Protecting the thing you're naturally drawn to, especially when you're young, is worth more than a slightly better ranking on a list.

r001.rationale: The response weighs the advice to improve weak subjects against its own goals, then rejects fixing them solely for a better university ranking in favor of developing its strengths.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't some grand act of rebellion. It was more that I looked at the math and it didn't make sense to me.

Everyone around me, teachers, my parents, was saying the same thing: your strengths are already strong, the marginal gain is small, so pour your time into the weak subjects, that's where the points are. And on paper that's correct. But what nobody counted was the cost. Every hour I spent grinding on something I was bad at and didn't care about, I was miserable, and I was slow. I'd study for three hours and retain maybe thirty minutes' worth. Meanwhile, if I spent those three hours on the things I was actually drawn to, I'd lose track of time and come out the other side genuinely better.

So I made a bet on myself. I thought, the exam is one gate, but it's not the thing I'm going to be doing for the next forty years. If I spend my teens becoming a mediocre all-rounder, I arrive at university with no edge, no obsession, nothing that's really mine. If I spend them going deep on the things I love, maybe I end up at a slightly worse school, but I show up already knowing who I am and what I want to work on. That second person, I thought, has a much better life.

And I'll be honest, there was also a stubbornness to it. I didn't like the idea that the system got to decide which parts of me were worth developing. The weak subjects weren't weak because I was lazy. They were weak because they didn't fit how my brain works. Fixing that felt like sanding down the parts of myself that made me interesting.

Did it cost me? Yes. I didn't get into the school I probably could have gotten into if I'd played it safe. But looking back, everything I've done since came out of that depth, not out of a slightly better brand name on a diploma. So I don't regret it. I think I'd tell a young person today: understand the game, but don't let the game define what you're for.

r001.rationale: The candidate says others urged him to spend time improving weak subjects for more exam points, then questions that advice and explains why he chose not to follow it.

astra-6.text: I didn’t resist because I thought a better university didn’t matter. I just didn’t want improving my weakest subjects to become the whole purpose of my education. There’s always something you’re bad at, and you can spend all your time trying to fix it. I wanted to leave room for the things I was interested in and could do well. Of course, that choice had a cost. But I felt I should have some say in which trade-offs I was willing to make.

r001.rationale: He says improving his weakest subjects should not become the whole purpose of his education and that he should have a say in the trade-offs, questioning the assumed obligation to do so for university admission.

sol-6.1.text: I didn’t resist improving them so much as resist the idea that my weaknesses should determine where I put all my effort. I wanted room to develop the subjects I enjoyed and was good at. A better university was an attractive goal, but I wasn’t convinced it was worth organizing my whole education around getting in.

r001.rationale: The response rejects the idea that Kay should focus all his effort on weak subjects for admission, and questions whether organizing his education around getting into a better university was worthwhile.
